title: Nkejje in Groundnut Paste
author: Maama Nakato
desc: Small sun-dried lake fish given a little roasting over an open fire and then served in a groundnut sauce — the standard treatment for a fish that arrives on the stick it was dried on.
longDesc: Nkejje are small broad-bodied fish from Lake Victoria, about six centimetres long, and the way they reach a market is part of the dish: caught in groups, dried in the sun immediately, pinned on sticks in horizontal rows, and carried to market on the same sticks after several days. They are commonly served in groundnut paste after a little roasting over an open fire. The fish plays a real ceremonial role in Buganda, particularly at child initiation and confirmation.
ingredients: Sun-dried nkejje — no quantity is given in the source
Cold water, to dissolve the paste
steps: Give the dried nkejje a little roasting over an open fire.
Dissolve the groundnut paste in cold water to a smooth thick sauce.
Bring the sauce to the boil and cook until it is ready.
Add the roasted nkejje and salt.
Simmer gently to bring the two together, and serve.
chefTips: A little roasting, not a proper cook. These are already dried through; the fire is for aroma and to firm them up before they go into a wet sauce.
Dissolve the groundnut paste in cold water first, as with every Ugandan groundnut sauce.
Add the fish after the sauce is made. Cooked in from the start they disintegrate.
No quantities are given in the source — this is prose rather than a numbered recipe, and nothing has been estimated to fill that.
Madoola are the largest and shiniest type of nkejje and are the ones to look for.
They come to market pinned on the sticks they were dried on, which is a good sign of freshness in the drying if the sticks are clean.
The fish is under real pressure — overfishing by commercial exporters, pollution, and the introduced Nile perch, which eats it.
The same sauce works with dried mukene, which is far easier to find.
commonMistakes: Roasting them hard until they burn.
Dissolving the groundnut paste in hot water.
Adding the fish at the start of the sauce.
Buying dried fish that smells ammoniac.
Over-simmering until nothing is left whole.
sources: Adapted from the nkejje entry, p37 of 'Traditional Products and Dishes: Uganda — From Earth to Table', second edition 2018, Slow Food International — the drying method (dried directly under the sun immediately after being caught, pinned on sticks in horizontal rows, carried to market on the same sticks after several days) and the preparation (commonly served in groundnut paste after a little roasting over an open fire) are as described there.
That entry is prose rather than a numbered recipe and gives no quantities. None has been estimated.

The physical description — about 6 centimetres head to tail and about 3 centimetres wide, with madoola the largest and shiniest type — the role in Buganda child initiation and confirmation ceremonies, and the threats of overfishing, pollution and Nile perch introduction are from the same entry.
storage: The dried fish keeps for months. The finished sauce, 3 days refrigerated.
reheating: Warm gently with a splash of water.
healthBenefits: Eaten whole with the bones, so very high in calcium.
High in protein, omega-3, iron and vitamin B12.
Groundnut paste adds plant protein and vitamin E.
culturalNote: Nkejje matters in Buganda beyond eating — it has a place in child initiation and confirmation ceremonies, and the lungfish mamba is one of the oldest totems of the kingdom's original clans. Lake Victoria's small fish carry ceremonial weight that the big commercial Nile perch, which eats them, does not.
